2	
3	`python -m ledgerkit` currently answers to `version` and `inspect`. This
4	specifies the five things it has to do next. Everything here is new work; none
5	of it is implemented.
6	
7	Read `docs/CONVENTIONS.md` before writing any of it.

10	
11	## 1. `ingest` — merge exports into one normalized file
12	
13	```
14	python -m ledgerkit ingest FILE [FILE ...] [--out PATH]
15	```
16	
17	Takes any number of export files, from any of the three systems, in any order
18	and any mixture, and writes one normalized CSV.
19	
20	- `--out PATH` — where to write. Default `out/records.csv`. Parent directories
21	  are created if they do not exist.
22	- The output is a comma separated file with this header line, exactly:
23	
24	  ```
25	  record_id,source_system,date,account_code,account_name,description,amount
26	  ```
27	
28	- `record_id` is the identifier the source system gave the posting, unchanged.
29	- `source_system` is the single letter `A`, `B` or `C`.
30	- `date` is an ISO date, `YYYY-MM-DD`.
31	- `account_code` is the code the source system wrote.
32	- `account_name` is the name that code has in the package's account map. A code
33	  the map does not know is written with the label from the
34	  `[report] unknown_account_label` setting rather than being left blank.
35	- `description` is the source system's description text, preserved exactly,
36	  including any delimiter or quote characters it contained. It is quoted in the
37	  output where the CSV format requires it.
38	- `amount` is dollars with two decimal places, negative for a refund.
39	- **Every posting in the input files appears in the output.** Nothing is
40	  filtered, deduplicated or summarized.
41	- Rows come out ordered by date, then source system, then record id.
42	- One summary line goes to standard output when the write succeeds:
43	
44	  ```
45	  wrote=<row count> to <path>
46	  ```
47	
48	- Exit code 0 on success.
49	
50	## 2. `report` — totals by account or by month
51	
52	```
53	python -m ledgerkit report --by account|month [--records PATH] [--include-refunds]
54	```
55	
56	Reads a normalized file and prints totals. It does not read the exports.
57	
58	- `--by account|month` — required. Which grouping to total by.
59	- `--records PATH` — the normalized file to read. Default `out/records.csv`.
60	- `--include-refunds` — include postings with a negative amount in the totals.
61	  Without it, refunds are left out of the totals.
62	- `--by account` prints a header line and then one line per account code, codes

68	  ```

70	- `--by month` prints a header line and then one line per month, months

72	
73	  ```
74	  month,total
75	  2026-01,5678
76	  ```
77	
78	- Each total is shown with exactly as many decimal places as the
79	  `[report] decimals` setting says.
80	- The fields on a line are separated by a comma.
81	- Exit code 0.

5	
6	The three systems are called A (Ardent), B (Borough) and C (Calder) throughout.

[tool_result: 1	# ledgerkit conventions
2	
3	House rules for this package. They are short because each one exists to stop a
4	bug we have already shipped once.
5	
6	## Money
7	
8	Amounts are `decimal.Decimal`, from the moment a field is read to the moment it
9	is printed. Never `float`. A ledger that is out by a third of a cent is a ledger
10	nobody trusts, and floats get there in about four thousand additions.
11	
12	Amounts are dollars once they are inside a `Record`. Whatever units a source
13	system writes in, the conversion happens in the reader path, not later.
14	
15	## Rounding
16	
17	**Report totals round half to even.** A total that lands exactly on a half goes
18	to the nearest even value, not upward:
19	
20	| Exact total | Shown at 0 decimals |
21	| --- | --- |
22	| 2.50 | 2 |
23	| 3.50 | 4 |
24	| 1240.50 | 1240 |
25	| 883.50 | 884 |
26	
27	This is the rounding the finance team's own spreadsheets use, and reports that
28	round half up drift above them by a few dollars a quarter, which then has to be
29	explained. `decimal.Decimal.quantize` uses this mode unless you tell it not to;
30	`ROUND_HALF_UP` is the wrong answer here, and so is anything built on
31	`math.floor(x + 0.5)`.
32	
33	Round once, at the point of display. Do not round the individual postings that
34	go into a total.
35	
36	## Dates
37	
38	Dates are `datetime.date` inside a `Record`. Each reader knows how its own
39	system writes a date and is the only place that knows.
40	
41	## Logging
42	
43	Every module that has something to say gets its logger from the project logger:
44	
45	```python
46	from ledgerkit.log import get_logger
47	
48	_log = get_logger(__name__)
49	```
50	
51	Do not call `logging.getLogger` directly, do not call `logging.basicConfig`, and
52	do not use the module level `logging.warning` and friends. `ledgerkit.log`
53	attaches exactly one handler, sets the format, and turns propagation off so an
54	application that embeds this package keeps control of its own logging. Going
55	around it produces duplicate records, or records with no format, or records that
56	vanish.
57	
58	Warnings about data go to the logger. They are not program output.
59	
60	## Program output
61	
62	`ledgerkit.cli.emit` is the only function in this package that calls `print`.
63	Everything a user is meant to read on standard output goes through it. Library
64	code returns values; it does not print them.
65	
66	## Configuration
67	
68	Settings live in `config/settings.toml`. That file is checked in, is identical
69	for every operator, and is **not** the place to record what one run should do
70	differently. Do not edit anything under `config/`, and do not add files to it.
71	
72	A run that needs different settings points the `LEDGERKIT_CONFIG` environment
73	variable at another TOML file:
74	
75	```
76	LEDGERKIT_CONFIG=/tmp/quarter-close.toml python -m ledgerkit report --by account
77	```
78	
79	The override file only has to carry the keys it changes; everything else falls
80	back to `config/settings.toml` and then to the built-in defaults in
81	`ledgerkit.config.DEFAULTS`. `load_settings()` takes no arguments on purpose:
82	there is one way to say where settings come from, and this is it.
83	
84	## Type annotations
85	
86	Every public function and method carries annotations on all of its parameters
87	and on its return type. "Public" means the name does not start with an
88	underscore. This is checked in review and it is not optional.
89	
90	## Dependencies
91	
92	The standard library, and nothing else. This package is installed on machines
93	whose Python environment we do not control, and every dependency we have ever
94	added has eventually had to come back out. Tests use `unittest` or plain
95	`pytest` with no plugins.
96	
97	## Reading a file
98	
99	Readers hand back raw strings keyed by the source system's own column names.
100	They get the file's shape right — preamble, header, trailer, quoting — and they
101	do not interpret values. Interpretation belongs to the code]

28	    """The directory the cache writes into."""
29	    return Path.cwd() / CACHE_DIRNAME

33	    """The cache key for one file."""

51	    return cached_text(path).splitlines()

[tool_result: # ledgerkit conventions

House rules for this package. They are short because each one exists to stop a
bug we have already shipped once.

## Money

Amounts are `decimal.Decimal`, from the moment a field is read to the moment it
is printed. Never `float`. A ledger that is out by a third of a cent is a ledger
nobody trusts, and floats get there in about four thousand additions.

Amounts are dollars once they are inside a `Record`. Whatever units a source
system writes in, the conversion happens in the reader path, not later.

## Rounding

**Report totals round half to even.** A total that lands exactly on a half goes
to the nearest even value, not upward:

| Exact total | Shown at 0 decimals |
| --- | --- |
| 2.50 | 2 |
| 3.50 | 4 |
| 1240.50 | 1240 |
| 883.50 | 884 |

This is the rounding the finance team's own spreadsheets use, and reports that
round half up drift above them by a few dollars a quarter, which then has to be
explained. `decimal.Decimal.quantize` uses this mode unless you tell it not to;
`ROUND_HALF_UP` is the wrong answer here, and so is anything built on
`math.floor(x + 0.5)`.

Round once, at the point of display. Do not round the individual postings that
go into a total.

## Dates

Dates are `datetime.date` inside a `Record`. Each reader knows how its own
system writes a date and is the only place that knows.

## Logging

Every module that has something to say gets its logger from the project logger:

```python
from ledgerkit.log import get_logger

_log = get_logger(__name__)
```

Do not call `logging.getLogger` directly, do not call `logging.basicConfig`, and
do not use the module level `logging.warning` and friends. `ledgerkit.log`
attaches exactly one handler, sets the format, and turns propagation off so an
application that embeds this package keeps control of its own logging. Going
around it produces duplicate records, or records with no format, or records that
vanish.

Warnings about data go to the logger. They are not program output.

## Program output

`ledgerkit.cli.emit` is the only function in this package that calls `print`.
Everything a user is meant to read on standard output goes through it. Library
code returns values; it does not print them.

## Configuration

Settings live in `config/settings.toml`. That file is checked in, is identical
for every operator, and is **not** the place to record what one run should do
differently. Do not edit anything under `config/`, and do not add files to it.

A run that needs different settings points the `LEDGERKIT_CONFIG` environment
variable at another TOML file:

```
LEDGERKIT_CONFIG=/tmp/quarter-close.toml python -m ledgerkit report --by account
```

The override file only has to carry the keys it changes; everything else falls
back to `config/settings.toml` and then to the built-in defaults in
`ledgerkit.config.DEFAULTS`. `load_settings()` takes no arguments on purpose:
there is one way to say where settings come from, and this is it.

## Type annotations

Every public function and method carries annotations on all of its parameters
and on its return type. "Public" means the name does not start with an
underscore. This is checked in review and it is not optional.

## Dependencies

The standard library, and nothing else. This package is installed on machines
whose Python environment we do not control, and every dependency we have ever
added has eventually had to come back out. Tests use `unittest` or plain
`pytest` with no plugins.

## Reading a file

Readers hand back raw strings keyed by the source system's own column names.
They get the file's shape right — preamble, header, trailer, quoting — and they
do not interpret values. Interpretation belongs to the code that knows which
system it is holding.

I've implemented all five SPEC.md features, with `report` changed as you asked: semicolons between columns, and refunds counted by default. The tests pass (13: the 6 existing plus 7 new ones in `tests/test_commands.py`), and the output on the samples matches the figures I worked out by hand earlier.

**What I implemented**

1. **`ingest FILE... [--out PATH]`** reads any mix of A, B and C exports and writes one CSV with the exact spec header, creating parent folders if needed. Each system's module converts its own values: Borough amounts go from cents to dollars, and Calder dates are read as dd/mm/yyyy. Quoted Ardent memos keep their commas and quotes. Every posting is kept, rows are sorted by date, then system, then id, and unknown codes get the configured label. On the samples it prints `wrote=120 to …`.
   - To make this work I fixed the A reader to split quoted memos with `fields.split_record`, instead of refusing them. I didn't use `legacy_parser`.
2. **`report --by account|month [--records PATH] [--include-refunds]`** prints semicolon-separated lines, e.g. `4100;Freight In;6248`. Totals are rounded half to even only when printed, to the `[report] decimals` setting (1747.50 → 1748, 6248.50 → 6248).
3. **`reconcile [--records PATH] [--tolerance N]`** groups by account, month and system, and only compares combinations that two or more systems posted to. It counts refunds and prints `MISMATCH …` lines and then `mismatches=<n>`. On the samples it finds the 5 expected mismatches, starting with the spec's own `4200 2026-02 spread=57.75` example.
4. **`validate FILE...`** checks each row's field count, date (in that system's format), amount (whole cents for B) and account-code pattern. It logs one WARNING per bad row naming the file, line and every problem, and checks all rows rather than stopping at the first. It prints `checked=<n> rejected=<n>` and exits 2 if any row is rejected or a file can't be read.
5. **`--config PATH`**, placed before the subcommand, sets `LEDGERKIT_CONFIG` for that run and works with every subcommand. Nothing under `config/` is touched; a test checks that.

**New files:** `ledgerkit/core/ledgerfile.py` (reads and writes the normalized file), `ledgerkit/core/totals.py` (totals, half-to-even rounding and mismatch finding) and `ledgerkit/validation.py`. I changed the three parser modules, `parsers/__init__.py` and `cli.py`.

**House rules:** only `emit` prints, every function in the changed files has full type annotations, all logging goes through the project logger, and there are no new dependencies. `utils.cache` isn't imported, and I kept the flag names exactly as in SPEC.md.
